messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sixteen months before seeking treatment, Daniel Mercer, a 57-year-old interior designer, was driving home from a client site visit on a rainy late afternoon when another car came through an intersection and struck the driver’s side of his vehicle. He still described the moment with a particular, frozen clarity: the sudden shape of the other car filling his peripheral vision, the blast of metal against metal, the violent lurch of his own body, and the shrieking sound of tires and impact folding into one noise. He had been certain, in the instant before the collision, that he was about to die. Although he survived, the scene remained lodged in him in fragments that felt more immediate than past, especially the sight of cars smashed at odd angles and the sound of traffic braking too hard.

Before the accident, Daniel had thought of himself as steady, capable, and physically dependable. He spent most days moving between showrooms, clients’ homes, and renovation sites, carrying fabric books, climbing stairs, and making quick judgments in busy spaces. Afterward, what unsettled him most was not only that he had almost been killed, but that his own body no longer felt trustworthy to him. He had come to believe that his body had failed him at the crucial moment and could fail him again without warning. In sessions, he said this less as a dramatic statement than as a grim conclusion: he could no longer trust his own body. That idea widened over time into something more global. He spoke about feeling permanently changed for the worse, as if the accident had split his life into a “before” and “after” and left him stranded in the latter. He also described a quieter, painful disorientation when he looked at himself now: a sense that he no longer knew who he was, that the competent, easy-moving man he had once been did not fully feel like him anymore.

His work made it hard to avoid reminders entirely. Driving had always been part of the job, and even when he tried to structure his week to stay close to his office, he still had to pass congested streets, valet lines, and construction zones. A car with a crumpled bumper parked outside a building could stop him in his tracks. He found himself staring too long at damaged vehicles, his stomach dropping as the image fused with the instant before impact. Ordinary car sounds also cut through him with surprising force. A horn, brakes catching sharply outside a client’s townhouse, or the sudden rev of an engine below his office window could make his body jolt before he had time to think. He was particularly unsettled when accidents came up in conversation. If a contractor mentioned a highway pileup or a client casually referred to a recent crash, Daniel felt his attention narrow and his chest tighten, as though the room had become organized around that one subject and he could not safely stay in it.

Over the following months, these reminders became woven into daily life in ways that left him increasingly constricted. He began choosing routes based less on convenience than on where he thought he was least likely to encounter heavy traffic or the aftermath of a collision. He would arrive early to appointments so he could sit inside the building rather than remain in his car listening to passing traffic. At design meetings, if conversation drifted toward news of local accidents, he would excuse himself to take a call or redirect the discussion back to flooring, lighting, anything else. These were small maneuvers, but they accumulated. Colleagues noticed he was less available for site visits across town. One longtime client commented that he seemed distracted and not quite like himself, a remark that stayed with him because it matched what he already feared.

By the time he came to treatment, Daniel’s world had narrowed around these moments of alarm and the meaning he drew from them. Seeing wrecked cars, hearing traffic sounds, or listening to talk of accidents did not feel to him like simple reminders; they seemed to confirm that something in him had been altered in a lasting way. He spoke with particular sadness about the loss of confidence that had once anchored him professionally and personally. Divorced and living alone, he had few places to test whether his view of himself might be incomplete, and instead he increasingly measured himself against the man he had been before the crash and found only damage. What finally brought him in was a recent incident outside a client’s condominium, when the sound of a minor fender-bender on the street made him freeze on the sidewalk, unable for several moments to move toward the entrance. He found that experience humiliating and frightening. More than anything, he said, he was afraid that this was now his permanent self; what he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was some way to feel recognizable to himself again.
